title: Bottom-Up Prediction of Amorphous Poly(1,3-dioxolane) using Ab Initio Reactive Machine-Learning Force Fields
authors: Yizhi Song, Bharatha K. Gunawardana, Kriti Alam, Teresa Shah, Deepa Ranabhat, Hsin-Yu Ko
abstract: Poly(1,3-dioxolane) (pDXL) is a chemically recyclable polyether that can be synthesized by living cationic ring-opening polymerization with precise control of chain length into the ultra-high-molecular-weight (UHMW) regime, where it acquires enhanced mechanical properties. Like most polymers, however, it has amorphous condensed-phase structure, and diffraction measurements alone cannot resolve the atomistic microstructure that underlies them. In this work, we predict the ensemble of the pDXL microstructures by applying a recently developed AI-accelerated ab initio bottom-up polymer structure prediction (AI$^{2}$-BPSP) framework that simulates the living polymerization of pDXL under experimental synthetic conditions with machine-learning force fields trained within van der Waals-corrected hybrid density functional theory. Partitioning the predicted X-ray and neutron diffraction signal between the growing chain and the surrounding monomer resolves its dominant feature into two counteracting modes: a monomer contribution near $q \approx 1.5$ Å$^{-1}$ that decays as monomer is consumed, and a polymer contribution near $q \approx 1.6$ Å$^{-1}$ that is absent in oligomers and grows with chain length. This work paves the way to direct accuracy validation of these statistically significant, first-principles, and chain-length resolved diffraction predictions against experiments.
summary: This work pioneers the use of AI-accelerated simulations to predict the atomic structure of amorphous polymers like pDXL by simulating their synthesis. By analyzing the resulting ensemble microstructures, the authors successfully deconvolute the measured diffraction signal into distinct contributions from the monomer and the growing polymer chain. This provides a powerful, first-principles method for validating polymer structure against experimental scattering data.
main_problem: The challenge is to determine the atomistic microstructure of amorphous Poly(1,3-dioxolane) (pDXL) and predict its experimentally measurable scattering signals.
main_result: The primary diffraction peak is revealed to be a sum of two counteracting modes: a decaying monomer contribution ($\approx 1.5 	ext{ Å}^{-1}$) and a growing polymer contribution ($\approx 1.6 	ext{ Å}^{-1}$).
method: The authors employed an AI-accelerated *ab initio* bottom-up polymer structure prediction (AI2-BPSP) framework to simulate the living cationic ring-opening polymerization.
model_or_system: The system is amorphous pDXL undergoing polymerization. The simulation uses a Machine-Learning Force Field trained on DFT data to model bond breaking and formation during the polymerization process.
key_observables: X-ray and neutron interference functions ($F_X(q)$, $F_N(q)$), partial radial distribution functions ($g_{\alpha eta}(r)$), and partial structure factors ($S_{\alpha eta}(q)$).
important_parameters: Chain length ($n$, up to 100-mer), temperature (300 K), and pressure (1 bar).
main_assumptions: The MLFF is assumed transferable from short oligomers to the macromolecular limit, and the ensemble is not assumed to be at true equilibrium due to finite simulation time.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the polymerization steps, partial radial distribution functions at various chain lengths, statistical convergence of structural metrics, and the predicted interference functions showing the separation of monomer and polymer contributions.
paper_structure: The paper details the AI2-BPSP workflow, simulating polymerization to generate ensembles of microstructures. It then analyzes the resulting structures by calculating partial structure factors and predicting the total X-ray and neutron scattering functions, emphasizing the separation of contributions from the monomer and the growing polymer backbone.
why_interesting: The use of ML-force fields trained on quantum mechanical data (DFT) to simulate complex, disordered polymer growth processes is highly relevant to ML-physics, providing a predictive tool for materials structure.
